items.title: Morning Briefing: Nov. 4, 2026
items.excerpt: Seyit Kurt 04 November 2026• Update: 04 November 2026 Here’s a rundown of all the news you need to start your Wednesday, including US Democrats projected to win both houses of Congress in midterm elections, US midterms delivering wave of historic firsts across states, and President Donald Trump’s pledging to end US financial aid to Israel by year’s end. Democrats were projected to take control of both chambers of the US Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections, delivering a major political setback to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party, according to US media projections. The party made significant gains beyond its traditional strongholds, winning key races in states that overwhelmingly supported Trump in the 2024 presidential election, including Texas, South Carolina, Ohio, Iowa, and Kansas. The scale of the Democratic wave was still becoming clear early Wednesday, but the results pointed to widespread voter dissatisfaction with the Trump administration, particularly over the economy, rising living costs, and the president's decision to launch a war against Iran in February. - US midterms deliver wave of historic firsts across states, Congress Tuesday’s US midterm elections produced a series of historic firsts in races for governor, Senate and the House of Representatives. In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor of any US state, as well as Georgia’s first woman and first Black governor. Former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland won in New Mexico to become the first Native American woman elected governor in US history, while Minnesota Democrat Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American woman elected to the US Senate. In New Jersey, Democrat Adam Hamawy won the 12th Congressional District to become the state’s first Muslim member of Congress. Texas Democrat Gina Hinojosa became the state’s first Latina governor, while Republican Byron Donalds was elected Florida’s first Black governor. In Ohio, Amy Acton became the state’s first woman and first Jewish governor, while David Crowley became Wisconsin’s first Black governor. Illinois Democrat Juliana Stratton’s Senate victory also means three Black women will serve simultaneously in the chamber for the first time. - Trump pledges end to US aid for Israel by year’s end US President Donald Trump said Tuesday that Washington will stop providing financial aid to Israel by year's end under an agreement reached with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. "Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping, and they're fine with it because, you know, they've become a very successful country that are not in need, and we won't be paying any more to Israel," Trump told Fox News. He added that Washington would still provide assistance if needed, describing Israel as a regional partner with whom the US has maintained "a tremendous relationship," with Tel Aviv being the smaller partner. ... - Spanish Transport Minister Oscar Puente announced his resignation after a high-speed train accident in Toledo killed 69 people and injured around 200 others last week, El Pais reported.

items.excerpt: ### The expected Blue wave crashes down on American Republicans in Midterms, Iran threatens to kill Trump and China looks to make progress in Middle East | Succinct, unbiased global news Stephen Wolfe - 10 Things News Nov 04, 2026 1. Democrats Win House And Make Historic Senate Gains (US) 2. Trump Says He Will Accept Midterm Election Results (US) 3. China Seeks Greater Role in Iran Diplomacy (Geopolitics) 4. Iran Displays Billboard Threatening Trump’s Life (Middle East) 5. Trump Announces End to US Military Aid for Israel (Middle East) 6. King Charles Stops Short of Slavery Apology (UK) 7. US and Canada Report Progress Towards Trade Deal (Trade) 8. Spanish Transport Minister Quits After Deadly Rail Crash (Europe) 9. Binance Details $6.3 Billion Crypto Theft (Finance) 10. Brazil Publishes Global Fossil Fuel Transition Roadmap (Climate) As we go to press Democrats have won control of the US House of Representatives and captured six Republican-held Senate seats with expectations that they will also win control of the Senate in Tuesday’s midterm elections, according to projections reported by major news organisations. Victories in Texas, Kansas, South Carolina, North Carolina, Iowa and Ohio put the party on course for a Senate majority, although races in Michigan and Minnesota remained important to the final balance. The results followed voter dissatisfaction with living costs and President Donald Trump’s war in Iran. Democrats also gained House seats in states including Indiana, New Jersey and Pennsylvania. US equity futures and the dollar fell as investors responded to the prospect of divided government. ... Trump said he would accept the results but blamed Republican losses on his absence from the ballot. He also threatened to veto Democratic legislation. The change in House control takes effect on 3 January, ending Republicans’ ability to pass legislation without Democratic support and giving Democrats investigative powers, including subpoenas. ###### Sources: Bloomberg, Wall Street Journal ... China has intensified diplomatic efforts across the Middle East as the prospect of renewed US attacks on Iran raises concerns among Gulf governments. Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted Oman’s Sultan Haitham bin Tariq in Beijing, while Foreign Minister Wang Yi held separate talks with senior Iranian and Saudi officials. Beijing also announced plans to dispatch three senior envoys to seven countries across the Middle East and Africa. Xi called for the region to avoid great power rivalry, while Wang urged negotiations rather than further armed conflict. The initiative comes as Gulf states seek to break the US-Iran deadlock. China has substantial economic interests at stake, including energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz, regional investments and export markets. Beijing also wants a greater role in shaping regional security arrangements, although its previous diplomatic initiatives have produced limited results. ... US President Donald Trump announced on Tuesday that Washington would end nearly $4 billion in annual military assistance to Israel by the end of 2026. Speaking during the US midterm elections, Trump said he had agreed the change with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, arguing that Israel no longer needed the funding. Trump suggested that arms sales would replace direct assistance. However, Israeli officials appeared surprised, and neither Netanyahu’s office nor Israel’s foreign minister immediately confirmed the agreement. The announcement also followed growing domestic criticism of US support for Israel, including from Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. Implementation remains uncertain because Congress appropriates the funding, limiting the president’s ability to terminate it unilaterally. Existing missile defence and weapons programmes also complicate an immediate withdrawal. Netanyahu had previously proposed phasing out American military assistance over a decade, making Trump’s proposed year-end deadline a substantial acceleration of that timetable. ... Spain’s Transport Minister Óscar Puente resigned on Tuesday, six days after a high-speed train collision near Urda, south of Madrid, killed at least 69 people. A moving train struck the rear of a stationary service following a signalling system failure. Puente told parliament that a transport minister could not remain in office after two serious accidents within a year. The October crash followed another deadly collision in January. Puente faced resignation demands from opposition parties and some government allies, while Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez acknowledged that confidence in Spain’s railway system had been broken. Puente also withdrew from the candidate lists for the early general election scheduled for 29 November. ... Hackers stole $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance after compromising employees through a fake job interview and tampered software, the exchange said on Tuesday. Its initial investigation traced the attack to June, when a wallet developer downloaded a manipulated tool. Binance detected that breach and replaced the device but information about the wallet team had been exposed. In September, another engineer downloaded malicious code during recruitment interviews with a fictitious company. The attackers subsequently used the compromised computer and an internal AI tool to access wallet developers’ systems, before deploying stolen credentials and a malicious script on October 29. The attackers transferred 233.46 million XRP from five internet-connected wallets in four minutes and continued removing assets for nearly four hours. Binance froze approximately $2.85 billion in assets and said it would reimburse affected customers. The FBI attributed the attack to a North Korean hacking group, an allegation Pyongyang denies. Brazil has published a global roadmap for moving away from fossil fuels, proposing steps countries can take without waiting for new technologies or economic changes. The non-binding plan, released by its Cop30 presidency on Tuesday, encourages governments to assess their dependence on coal, oil and gas before choosing measures suited to their circumstances. Recommendations include reducing gas flaring and venting, cutting fossil fuel subsidies and expanding renewable electricity. Brazil also published a separate roadmap to halt and reverse deforestation. That document identifies major financing gaps, with annual forest funding estimated at $85 billion against projected needs of $300 billion by 2030. Cop30 president André Corrêa do Lago said the aim was to shift climate talks towards implementing existing commitments. The fossil fuel roadmap offers possible actions rather than compulsory targets.

items.title: Strong US GDP Growth Comes With Higher Inflation
items.excerpt: The US economy posted stronger-than-expected growth in the third quarter, but accelerating inflation added to the economic challenges facing President Donald Trump as the midterm elections take place. ... Real gross domestic product (GDP) increased at an annualized rate of 3.4% between July and September, beating market expectations, the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) said. The growth rate was higher than the 2.2% recorded in the second quarter. The BEA attributed the expansion to increases in investment, consumer spending and government spending, partly offset by a decline in exports. The figures presented a mixed picture for policymakers and voters, as stronger economic activity coincided with persistent price pressures. The Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, rose 3.6% year over year in September, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, the PCE price index increased 0.5% in September, according to the BEA's report on personal income and outlays. Core PCE inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose 3.1% from a year earlier, compared with 3.0% in August. The acceleration in inflation could complicate the Federal Reserve's efforts to bring price increases back toward its 2% target, particularly as the economy continues to expand. The economic figures also come at a politically sensitive time for Trump. ... Voters are set to cast ballots in the November 3 midterm elections, with inflation, household expenses and the broader economy among the central issues. Democrats are seeking to regain control of both chambers of Congress from the president's Republican Party, making economic performance a significant factor in the election campaign.

items.title: The Fed can't fix this inflation. It's a mechanical weight, not a demand problem
items.excerpt: 11/02/2026 16:28:22 GMT # The Fed can't fix this inflation. It's a mechanical weight, not a demand problem Joshua Gibson FXStreet Producer prices are rising 2.6 points faster than consumer prices, the widest gap since 2022, because most of the Iran war's costs haven't reached shoppers yet. The part that has is fuel, and rate hikes can't make fuel cheaper. The Producer Price Index (PPI), which tracks what US businesses get for the goods and services they sell, rose 6.3% through September. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 3.7%. In February, the last full month before the Iran war, the gap between them was about a point. It's now 2.6 points, the widest since April 2022. Most of the war's costs still fall on businesses, and shoppers pay at the pump. The Federal Reserve (Fed) raised its rate to 3.75-4.00% in September and held it in October, with two members voting for another hike. The number that matters most for inflation is the price of Brent, the main global Oil price, and no one at the Fed sets it. ## Seven months of war, a tenth of a point outside energy Energy prices, which cover gasoline and the power and fuel used in homes, rose 20.4% through September, and gasoline alone rose 34.2%. Energy makes up about 7% of the CPI, so it added about 1.3 percentage points to the 3.7% total. In February it added almost nothing. Everything else barely changed. Prices outside food and energy, often called underlying inflation, were up 2.6%, a tenth of a point faster than in February. Food prices are rising more slowly than they were before the war. So almost all of the 1.3-point rise in inflation since February is the fuel bill, and with Brent trading near its highest since mid-2022, that bill hasn't gone away.

items.title: Stocks wilt, dollar slides as early midterm results point to blue sweep | MarketScreener UK
items.excerpt: Published on 11/04/2026 at 03:50 am GMT - Modified on 11/04/2026 at 05:43 am GMT ... SINGAPORE, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Global stocks slumped, and the dollar softened on Wednesday as Democrats scored a decisive win in the US midterm elections, fuelling fears the blue sweep could disrupt the data-centre buildout that has powered the AI trade and hurt tech spending. In a major setback to President Donald Trump and Republicans, Democrats notched stunning victories in the South Carolina, Texas and Ohio Senate races, capturing majorities in both the Senate and House that reached deep into Republican strongholds. The breadth of the party's success was underscored by gains in districts long considered safely conservative, highlighting a political shift that caught many investors off guard. The reaction from investors was to sell stocks, especially AI-linked shares, putting the dollar under pressure, while cryptocurrencies fell at the prospect of stronger regulations. Bonds, though, found favour as investors sought safety. Futures for the S&P 500 slid 0.6% while Nasdaq futures fell more than 2% before cutting losses to trade down 0.8%. The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note fell 6 basis points to 4.906%, pushing the dollar sharply lower. [FRX/]

items.title: Democrats flip four governorships, extending the party’s inroads into red states
items.excerpt: Democratic candidates flipped control of governorships in four races while maintaining power in several other states, further punctuating the party’s success in Tuesday’s elections. Seizing on a broadly toxic political climate for Republicans, Democrats notched victories in perennial battleground and deep red states across the map. Democratic candidates wrested control of governor’s mansions in Georgia, Iowa, Texas and Ohio. The most shocking flip came in Texas — a state Donald Trump won two years ago by nearly 14 points, where the last Democratic governor was elected more than three decades ago. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa defeated three-term GOP Gov. Greg Abbott, overcoming a massive spending deficit to become the state’s first Latina chief executive. ... Democrats also made history in Georgia, where former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated Republican Rick Jackson, flipping control of the battleground state office for the first time in 24 years. Bottoms’ victory means she will become the first Black female governor in U.S. history. Bottoms is one of three Black gubernatorial candidates who won Tuesday, along with Democratic Gov. Wes Moore in Maryland and Republican Byron Donalds in Florida. There has never been more than one Black governor serving at a time before. In Iowa, State Auditor Rob Sand beat Republican Zach Lahn, making him the first Democrat to be elected to lead the state in two decades. Trump won Iowa in 2024 by 13 points. And in Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton beat Republican businessman Vivek Ramaswamy, succeeding Republican Mike DeWine.

items.title: Missouri voters block Republican-drawn congressional map
items.excerpt: Missouri voters blocked a GOP-drawn congressional map from going into effect for future elections via a ballot measure, NBC News projects. The result is a blow for Republicans, who fought for more than a year to carve up one of the state’s two-Democratic-held districts. The vote was the culmination of a long-running political and legal fight. Missouri is one of the GOP-led states that heeded President Donald Trump’s mid-decade redistricting call, passing new lines last year that drew longtime Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver into a heavily Republican district. In response, a group called People Not Politicians Missouri said it gathered more than 300,000 signatures — well above the 106,000 necessary — to place a referendum on the ballot that gave voters the opportunity to veto the map. Legislation facing such a referendum is typically put on hold until voters have weighed in, but Missouri Republicans fought to put the map in place for this year’s midterms. State Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, waited until the statutory deadline in August to announce that he wouldn’t certify the referendum for the November ballot, saying it was unconstitutional. The issue ricocheted through the state and federal court systems, at times producing conflicting rulings. Ultimately, the U.S. Supreme Court rejected Missouri Republicans’ attempts to use the redrawn map for this year’s elections three times.
